passage:
After dinner, Jomon stood on the living room carpet with a folded paper. Neelam didi sat on the sofa, Mummy at the table, Papa with his tea.
Jomon: My poem is called 'Rain on the Roof'. Ready? Rain-on-the-roof-rat-a-tat...
Neelam: Slow down! We can't catch a word.
Jomon: Sorry. Rain on the roof, rat-a-tat-tat...
Papa: Look up from the paper, Jomon. Look at us.
Mummy: And pause after each verse.
Jomon tried again, slower, eyes up. Neelam clapped. "Now I can hear the rain," she said. He practised twice more, and on the day of the recital he did not rush at all.

qa.a: The poem is called 'Rain on the Roof'.

qa.a: Jomon is probably nervous but willing, since he tries again after each tip and grows steadier.

qa.q: How does Neelam see Jomon's poem after the tips?
qa.a: Neelam said 'Now I can hear the rain', so Neelam finds the slower version clearer and enjoys it more.

subtype: Approach: rehearsing in front of a mirror or family [Action]
passage: Two weeks before the Hindi recitation, I made my family my audience. Every night after dinner, Amma, my aunt Manjula and Dadi sat on the sofa, and I stood by the TV and recited. The first night I raced through all four verses and finished out of breath. Dadi said, "Slow down, my boy. We are not catching a train." Manjula Aunty said, "And look at us, Sachin, not at the floor." It was hard. When I looked up I forgot words. But each night I went a bit slower and lifted my eyes a bit more. On the day, I saw the judges' faces and didn't panic, because I'd practised looking at faces all week.

qa.q: Who sat on the sofa as Sachin's audience?
qa.a: Amma, Manjula Aunty and Dadi sat on the sofa.

qa.q: How did Sachin feel after racing through the first night?
qa.a: Sachin felt out of breath and flustered, and looking up at first made the words slip away.

qa.q: What else could Sachin practise if family is not free, and why?
qa.a: Sachin could recite to a mirror or a row of toys, because any audience helps Sachin practise looking up while speaking.

qa.q: How might the practice nights look to Dadi?
qa.a: Dadi sees Sachin rushing and gives gentle advice, and is likely proud to watch the slower, steadier recitation grow each night.

grounding: It shows a boy practising his poem before family after dinner, taking their advice to slow down and look up, and improving before the day.

subtype: Approach: rehearsing in front of a mirror or family [Action]
passage:
Note for Vishal's class teacher
Madam, Vishal has practised his English poem at home every evening this week, and I wanted you to know how hard he has worked. After dinner he stood at the end of the dining table and recited to me, his grandfather and his little sister. On Monday he spoke very fast and looked at his feet the whole time. His grandfather told him to breathe after each line and look at one face. By Wednesday he was slower. On Thursday he looked at his sister while reciting, and she clapped at the funny verse. He has asked to do it one more time on Friday morning before school. Please give him a smile from the front row if you can.
- Hafsa, Vishal's mother

qa.q: Who did Vishal recite to after dinner?
qa.a: He recited to his mother, his grandfather and his little sister.

qa.q: How did Vishal feel when his sister clapped at the funny verse?
qa.a: He probably felt encouraged and more confident, seeing that his audience was enjoying it.

qa.q: What else could help Vishal on the day of the recitation?
qa.a: He could pick one friendly face in the hall, like the teacher in the front row, to look at, the way he looked at his sister.

qa.q: How does the practice look to Vishal's grandfather?
qa.a: The grandfather sees a boy rushing and gives a simple tip, and is probably pleased to see it work by midweek.

grounding: It shows a boy rehearsing a poem in front of his family, who tell him to slow down and look up, and his improvement before the day.
